ĕgō^ (ŏ always in poets of the best age, as Cat., Verg., Hor., etc.; ō ante-class. and post-Aug., as ; , v. Corss. Ausspr. 2, 483;
gen. mei; dat. mihi; acc. and abl. me; plur., nom., and acc. nos; gen., mostly poet., nostrum; gen. obj. nostri, rarely nostrum; for the gen. possess. the adj. noster was used, q. v.; cf. Roby, Gram. 1, § 388; dat. and abl. nobis; mi in dat. for mihi, part., ; ; ; in prose,; et saep.; old form also MIHEI, C. I. L. 1, 1016 al.; v. Neue, Formenl. 2, 180; old form of the acc. MEHE, acc. to ; ; ; ; gen. plur. nostrorum, ; ; ; id. Am. Fragm. ap. ; dat. and abl. NIS = nobis, acc. to Fest. S. V. CALLIM, p. 47, 3 Müll.; acc. ENOS, Carm. Arval., Wordsworth, Fragm. and Spec. p. 160.—But as to me = mihi, cited in Müll., me is there not dat., but acc., v. Vahl. ad ), pron. pers. [Gr. ἐγώ; Sanscr. aham; Goth. ik; Germ. ich; Engl. I, etc.; plur. nos; Gr. νῶϊ, νῶϊν, from same stem with acc. sing. me, ], I.
Prop.: meruimus et ego et pater de vobis,: tum te audes Sosiam esse dicere, Qui ego sum?; cf.: ego tu sum, tu es ego: unanimi sumus,; the combination alter ego v. under alter.—
Emphasized.
By the suffixes met and pte: Am. Quis te verberavit? So. Egomet memet, : credebam primo mihimet Sosiae,: quasi per nebulam nosmet scimus,: med erga,: cariorem esse patriam nobis quam nosmetipsos, et saep.: mihipte, Cato ap. : mepte fieri servom,.—
By repetition: meme ad graviora reservat, (but , is written me, me); cf.: met and pte.—
Esp. to be noted are,
Mihi and nobis as dativi ethici (Zumpt Gr. § 408; A. and S. Gr. § 228 N.): quid enim mihi L. Pauli nepos quaerit,; cf. ; ; and in the plur.: quid ait tandem nobis Sannio?: sit mihi (orator) tinctus litteris, etc.,; cf. Liv. praef. § 9; 2, 29 fin.; ; ; ; ; Drak.; and in the plur.: nobis jam paulatim accrescere puer incipiat,: hic mihi Q. Fufius pacis commoda memorat,; cf. Kritz; : tu mihi seu magni superas jam saxa Timavi, etc., et saep.—
Mecum, nobiscum (v. cum, II. fin.).—
Ad me veni, i. e. ad meam domum, , v. ad, A. 2. a.
. —
Nos, etc., for ego, etc., in grave or official lang., etc.: nobis consulibus,; ; cf. ; so with sing. constr.: nec merito nobis inimica merenti,; cf. : absente nobis,; .

la:verb:egeo.gloss: to lack, to want, to be without
senses: to lack, to want, to be without
to desire, to long for, to want
la:verb:egeo.html:
ĕgĕo, ŭi, 2 (
part. fut. egitura, ), v. n.
cf. Gr. ἀχήν, poor; root αχ-, αγχ, in ἄχος, ἄγχω, etc.; Lat. angustus,

angina

, to be needy (for syn. cf.: indigeo, careo, vaco).
Prop.
Absol. (so usually in Plaut. and Ter.), to be needy, to be in want, to be poor: me in divitiis esse agrumque habere, egere illam autem,; cf. ; ; ; ; ; ; (opp. locupletem esse); (opp. dives); ; et saep.—Pass. impers.: amatur atque egetur acriter,.—
To need, want, lack, to be in need of, with the thing needed.
In the abl.: earum rerum, quibus egeremus, invectio,; cf. ; : omnibus necessariis rebus,: copiis,: oculis ad cernendum,: bibliothecis Graecis,; cf. : medicină,: nullo,: consilio, opera nostra,fin.: auxilio,: sapiens eget nulla re: egere enim necessitatis est, (cf. I. a. supra).—Of inanimate subjects: opus eget exercitatione non parva,; cf. ; ; et saep.—
In the gen. (in Cic. dub., v.the foll.): si pudoris egeas,: tui, admonitricis,; cf. ; : auxilii,: medicinae (al. medicina; cf. the preced.),: medici, curatoris,; cf. custodis,: aeris (opp. locuples mancipiis),: nullius,: nutricis,: alienae facundiae,—Of inanimate subjects: nec prosum quicquam nostrae rationis egere,; ; ; —
In the acc.: nec quicquam eges,; cf. the foll.—
Supplied by inf. pass.: clariores quam ut indicari egeant, Athenae,; cf. .
Sometimes transf.
(For the usual careo.) To be without, to be destitute of, not to have: C. Macer auctoritate semper eguit,: donis tuis, somne,.—Of inanimate subjects: res proprio nomine,. —*
To do without, to bear the want of: si quid est, quod utar, utor; si non est, egeo, Cato ap. .—
Like the Gr. δέομαι (cf. also the Engl. to want), to desire, wish for: tui amans abeuntis egeo,: plausoris,: tantuli,; cf. in the abl.: pane,.—Hence, ĕgens, entis, P. a., needy, necessitous, in want, very poor (class.; cf.: egenus, indigens, indigus, inops, pauper, mendicus): quocirca (amici) et absentes assunt egentes abundant,; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. opp. locuples,; ; opp. abundans,: delectus egentium ac perditorum,; cf. ; .— Comp.: nihil rege egentius,.—Sup.: egestates tot egentissimorum hominum,; ; ; opp. locuples,.—Adv. does not occur.

la:verb:egero.gloss: to carry, bear or bring out or away
senses: to carry, bear or bring out or away
la:verb:egero.html:
ē-gĕro, gessi, gestum, 3, v. a.,
to carry, bear or bring out, to lead or draw out, to discharge (not ante-Aug.).
Lit.: praedam ex hostium tectis, Drak.; cf. ; : pecuniam ex aerario,: fluctus (e navi),: stercus e columbariis,: humanas opes a Veiis,: humum scrobibus,; : tantum nivis,: silices umeris,, 4, 21, § 71: aquam vomitu,to discharge, void, vomit,; cf. dapes,: urinam,: sanguinem,; : multum vitalis spiritus,: viscera sua,.—Of inanimate subjects: gravitas caeli egerit populos,drives out, drives forth,.—
Poet. for efferre (I. B. 1.), to carry to the grave: (Phoebus) egessit avidis Dorica castra (i. e. Graecos) rogis (dat.), sent the Greeks to the funeral piles; acc. to others, exhausted, made empty the Grecian camp, ; .—
Trop.: tales pietas paritura querelas Egerit, pours forth, prodit, ; cf.: iras ululatibus,: sermones, i. q. edere,: expletur lacrimis egeriturque dolor,is expelled,: tota querelis Egeritur fletuque dies,i. e. is passed, spent,: noctem metu,: animam,.

la:verb:egredior.gloss: to go or come out or forth; march or step out
senses: to go or come out or forth; march or step out
to go beyond, pass out of or leave somewhere
la:verb:egredior.html:
ē-grĕdĭor, gressus, 3 (
inf. egredier, ), v. dep. n. and a.
Neutr., to go or come out, come forth (class.).
Lit.
In gen., with e or ex: foras e fano,; cf.: e fano huc,: e cubiculo,: ex oppido,; : ex suis finibus,: ex castris,: e curia,; et saep.—With a or ab: ab sese,; ; ; ; ; cf.: a nobis foras,. —With simple abl.: domo,: portă,; ; : Romă,; ; cf. ; : tabernaculo,: triclinio, et saep.; cf.: domo foras,.—With adv.: hinc,: intus,: unde, et saep.—Absol.: placide egredere,; so ; ; et saep.: foras,; ; ; ; et saep.: obviam,: per medias hostium stationes,; cf. poet.: per Veneris res,: extra munitiones,; ; : extra fines, terminos, cancellos,: extra portam,; cf.: ad portam, i. e. out to the gate. id.

33, 47 fin.: in vadum, et saep.—

In an upward direction, to go up, climb, mount, ascend: scalis egressi, Kritz.; cf.: ad summum montis,: in tumulum,: in altitudinem,: in vallum,: in tectum,: in moenia,: in sublime (liquor),: altius,.—
In partic.
Milit. t. t.
To step out, leave: ne quispiam ordine egrederetur,.—
To move out, march out: e castris,; : castris,; .—Absol., ; ; ; cf. also: in pacata,: ad proelium,: ad oppugnandum,.—
Naut. t. t.
(Ex) navi or absol., to disembark from a vessel, to land: ex navi,; ; : navi,; ; cf. ratibus,; and absol., ; ; ; cf.: in terram,; : in litus,.—
E portu, or absol., to set sail, ; ; .—
Trop. in speaking, to digress, depart, deviate, wander (rarely): a proposito ornandi causa,; cf.: ex quibus,.—Absol., : extra praescriptum,.
Act., to go beyond, to pass out of, to leave (freq. in the historians, partic. since the Aug. per.; not ante-class., nor in Cic.).
Lit.: fines,: munitiones nostras,: flumen Mulucham,: urbem,; fin.; 22, 55 fin. al.: tecta,: tentoria,; et saep.: navem, Oud. N. cr.: portum (navis),. —
Trop., to overstep, surpass, exceed: per omnia fortunam hominis egressus,; so, vetus familia neque tamen praeturam egressa,yet had attained no higher honor than,: quintum annum,: modum,; ; : sexum,fin.: clementiam majorum suasque leges,: relationem,: medios metus, et saep.: tecta altitudinem moenium egressa,

la:adj:egregius.html:
ē-grĕgĭus, a, um (
sup.: mulier egregiissimă formă, Pac. ap. P.; R: egregiissime grammatice,.—Vocat.: egregi or egregie,), adj.
ex-grex, Corss. Ausspr. 1, 504; hence, chosen from the herd, i. e.
, distinguished, surpassing, excellent, eminent (for syn. cf.: praeclarus, eximius, divinus, magnificus).
In gen. (class.): in procuratione civitatis, egregius,; cf.: in bellica laude,: in aliis artibus,: vir,: civis,: poëta,: senatus,: par consulum,: Caesar,; et saep.: et praeclara indoles ad dicendum,; cf. ; : forma,; cf. facies,: colores, odores,; : corpus,i. e. exceedingly beautiful,; : os, et saep.: virtus,: fides,: voluntas in se,: victoria, et saep.: vir bello egregius,; cf. ; ; .—With gen.: animi,; so, fati mentisque : linguae,: egregii juvenum,.—In the neutr. subst.: ut alia magna et egregia tua omittam,: postquam cuncta scelerum suorum pro egregiis accipi videt,for distinguished acts,; cf. the foll.—
Post - Aug., esp. of rank and consequence, distinguished, illustrious, honorable: si te privatus adoptarem, et mihi egregium erat Gnaei Pompeii subolem in penates meos asciscere, et, etc.,, 15; cf.: idque et sibi et cunctis egregium,.—Subst.: ēgrĕgĭum, ii, n.: egregium publicum,the public honor,—Hence, Egrĕgĭus, ii, m., a title of public officers in high station, similar to His Excellency, Cod. Th. 6, 22, 1; and: Vir Egregius,; et saep.; cf. —Hence, adv.: ēgrĕgĭe, excellently, eminently; surpassingly, exceedingly, singularly; uncommonly well (cf.: eximie, unice, praesertim ; praecipue, maxime, potissimum, etc.).
With verbs: studere (opp. mediocriter),: pingere, fingere,: loqui,: vincere,brilliantly,; cf. absolvi, et saep.—Far more freq.,
With adjectives: egregie cordatus homo, Enn. ap. (Ann. v. 335 ed. Vahl.): fortis et bonus imperator,: subtilis scriptor,: munitum oppidum,; cf. ; 5, 11, 7 et saep.—
Absol., as an expression of assent, applause, etc.: egregie, Caesar, quod lacrimas parentum vectigales esse non pateris,; cf. .—Comp.: egregius cenat,.
